summary: This RFC defines the Heartbeat Extension for TLS and DTLS. It adds a keep-alive protocol that avoids renegotiation and provides a basis for path MTU discovery in DTLS. The extension later became widely known because of a serious implementation bug in a popular library.

eli5.summary: Imagine tapping a friend on the shoulder to check they are still listening, without starting the whole conversation over. That is what this does for a secure connection.

questions: what is the heartbeat in tls
what is the tls heartbeat extension
subtitle: A keep-alive and probing message for TLS and DTLS that works without renegotiating.

tldr.problem: DTLS has no cheap way to check that a peer is alive or to probe the path MTU, and TLS has no built-in keep-alive without continuous data transfer.
tldr.mechanism: A new Heartbeat protocol sends a HeartbeatRequest carrying a payload and at least 16 bytes of random padding. The peer must answer with a HeartbeatResponse holding an exact copy of the payload.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can check liveness, keep NAT state fresh and send padded probes for path MTU discovery. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 8447.

today: RFC 6520 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8447.

sections.title: Why a Heartbeat
sections.content:
DTLS secures traffic over unreliable transports, which usually have no session management. The only way at the DTLS layer to tell whether a peer is alive is a costly renegotiation, particularly when traffic flows one way. DTLS also needs path MTU (PMTU) discovery but has no message type to do it without disturbing user messages. TLS runs on reliable transports, but nothing guarantees a way to keep a connection alive without continuous data transfer.

The Heartbeat Extension adds a HeartbeatRequest message that the peer must answer with a HeartbeatResponse. For PMTU discovery, requests containing padding serve as probe packets, as described in RFC 4821.
sections.eli5: Secure connections had no simple "are you still there?" button. This adds one.

sections.title: Agreeing to Use Heartbeats
sections.content:
Support is announced with a Hello extension holding a HeartbeatMode. The value peer_allowed_to_send (1) says the endpoint will receive requests and respond. The value peer_not_allowed_to_send (2) says it only wants to send them. The choice can change with every renegotiation.

A request MUST NOT be sent to a peer that indicated peer_not_allowed_to_send. If such an endpoint receives one anyway, it SHOULD drop it silently and MAY send an unexpected_message alert. An unknown mode MUST get an illegal_parameter alert in response.
sections.eli5: Before you start tapping shoulders, each side says whether it is happy to be tapped or only wants to do the tapping.

sections.title: How the Protocol Behaves
sections.content:
Heartbeat is a new protocol running on top of the Record Layer with two message types: heartbeat_request (1) and heartbeat_response (2). A request can arrive almost any time and SHOULD be answered. It SHOULD NOT be sent during handshakes, and a receiver SHOULD silently discard one that arrives mid-handshake. For DTLS, requests from older epochs SHOULD be discarded.

There MUST NOT be more than one request in flight at a time. It stays in flight until the matching response arrives or the retransmit timer expires.

Over unreliable transports such as UDP or DCCP, requests MUST be retransmitted using the DTLS flight timeout scheme from RFC 6347, and after a number of retransmissions without a response the connection SHOULD be terminated. Together with the one-in-flight rule, this handles congestion control. Over reliable transports such as TCP or SCTP, a request is sent once, and the application MAY terminate the connection if no response comes after some time.
sections.eli5: You only ask one question at a time and wait for the answer. If the line is shaky you ask again a few times, and if nobody ever answers you hang up.

sections.title: The Heartbeat Message
sections.content:
Each message has a 1-byte type, a 2-byte payload_length, the payload and then padding. The total length MUST NOT exceed 2^14 or the negotiated max_fragment_length. The padding must be at least 16 bytes of random content, and the receiver MUST ignore it.

The receiver of a request MUST reply with a response carrying an exact copy of the request payload. If payload_length is too large for the received message, the message MUST be discarded silently. A response without the expected payload MUST also be discarded silently; one with the expected payload stops the retransmission timer.
sections.eli5: You send a short note and some random filler. The other side must write your note back exactly, and everyone ignores the filler.

sections.title: Use Cases and Security
sections.content:
Each direction is independent: an endpoint should not expect its peer to send requests. For path MTU discovery, the padded requests are the probe packets, much like the padding chunk used in SCTP (RFC 4820).

For a liveness check, requests show the peer is reachable, even over TLS/TCP at a much higher rate than TCP keep-alive allows, and they refresh the state of NATs on the path. They SHOULD be sent only after an idle period of at least multiple round-trip times. That idle period SHOULD be configurable from one second up to multiple minutes, with a default that is tunable per peer.

The security considerations of RFC 5246 and RFC 6347 apply, and the RFC says it introduces no new ones.
sections.eli5: You can tap to check the friend is there, to keep the doorway open, or to test how big a package fits down the hall.

fields.name: payload
fields.desc: Arbitrary content, variable length; copied back in the response.

fields.name: padding
fields.desc: Random content, at least 16 bytes; ignored by the receiver.
